title: Weak factorization systems on finite direct diagrams
statement: Let $\mathcal B$ be a cocomplete category (one admitting every small colimit [def-weil-pbc-category-colimit]) and let $(\mathcal L,\mathcal R)$ be a weak factorization system with functorial factorizations: every map factors functorially as a map in $\mathcal L$ followed by a map in $\mathcal R$, and each class is exactly the maps with the diagonal-lifting property against the other. Let $K$ have finitely many objects and morphisms and a natural-number degree strictly increased by nonidentity arrows. For $X:K\to\mathcal B$ set $L_kX=\operatorname{colim}_{(a:j\to k)\ne1_k}X_j$, with morphisms in the indexing category the commuting triangles over $k$. For $f:X\to Y$ let $\lambda_k(f):X_k\coprod_{L_kX}L_kY\to Y_k$. Then the maps for which all $\lambda_k(f)$ belong to $\mathcal L$, together with the maps that are objectwise in $\mathcal R$, form a weak factorization system with functorial factorizations on $\operatorname{Fun}(K,\mathcal B)$. Every map in its left class is objectwise in $\mathcal L$, and its colimit map is in $\mathcal L$. This includes empty $K$ and also applies with any other finite direct category in place of $K$.

source.place: Hovey, Model Categories, Section 5.1, Proposition 5.1.4, Corollary 5.1.5 and proof of Theorem 5.1.3, printed pp. 121-122. The factorization and lifting induction uses only the specified weak factorization system, not both systems or weak equivalences. No Stacks tag states this diagram-WFS extension.

proof.text: Use functional composition. Write $D_k$ for the full subcategory of $K/k$ of nonidentity arrows, and $K_{<n}$ for the full subcategory on objects of degree less than $n$. Every object $(j,a)$ of $D_k$ has $\deg j<\deg k$, and every nonidentity arrow in $D_k$ increases this domain degree. The categories are finite, including their morphisms. All latching objects and all pushouts therefore exist by cocompleteness and [def-weil-pbc-category-colimit]. Fix colimit cocones once. Maps of diagrams induce maps of latching objects by their compatible components; their identity and composition laws follow by testing on the colimit coprojections. The canonical maps $L_kX\to X_k$ and $L_kY\to Y_k$ commute with $f$, so the pushout universal property gives $\lambda_k(f)$. Put $C_K=\{f:\lambda_k(f)\in\mathcal L\text{ for all }k\}$ and $R_K=\{p:p_k\in\mathcal R\text{ for all }k\}$.

source.place: Section 5.1, definition of latching objects, printed pp. 120-121; finite-degree specialization; Stacks 002F (categories-definition-colimit) for all universal properties.

proof.text: Construct a factorization $f=pi$ by induction on $n$, with a diagram $Z$ and natural transformations $X\xrightarrow{i}Z\xrightarrow{p}Y$ on $K_{<n}$. At $n=0$ these are the empty diagrams. To add an object $k$ of degree $n$, the already defined diagram supplies $L_kZ$ and a map $L_kX\to L_kZ$. The maps $X_k\xrightarrow{f_k}Y_k$ and $L_kZ\xrightarrow{L_kp}L_kY\to Y_k$ agree on $L_kX$ by naturality of the previously constructed factorization. Thus form $P_k=X_k\coprod_{L_kX}L_kZ\to Y_k$ and apply the specified functorial factorization in $\mathcal B$ to obtain $P_k\xrightarrow{\ell_k}Z_k\xrightarrow{p_k}Y_k$ with $\ell_k\in\mathcal L$ and $p_k\in\mathcal R$. Define $i_k$ by the $X_k$ coprojection. For a nonidentity $a:j\to k$, define $Z(a)$ by $Z_j\to L_kZ\to P_k\xrightarrow{\ell_k}Z_k$. If $h:t\to j$ is another arrow, the equality of the coprojection indexed by $ah$ with the coprojection indexed by $a$ composed with $Z(h)$ proves $Z(ah)=Z(a)Z(h)$. The two coprojections of $P_k$ prove naturality of $i,p$ on these arrows, and $p_ki_k=f_k$. There are no nonidentity arrows between objects of degree $n$, so these choices extend the induction simultaneously. A bound for the finitely many degrees terminates the construction. Since the full latching diagram at $k$ was already present when $k$ was added, $\lambda_k(i)=\ell_k$ under the fixed pushout choices. Consequently $i\in C_K$, $p\in R_K$.

source.place: Proof of Theorem 5.1.3, printed p. 122, functorial factorization induction, applied to only the given WFS.

proof.text: For functoriality, let $(u,v):f\to f'$ be a square of natural transformations. Assume by induction that the comparison $Z_j\to Z'_j$ has been defined naturally on $K_{<n}$. Its latching colimit map and $u_k$ give $P_k\to P'_k$, commuting with the maps to $Y_k\xrightarrow{v_k}Y'_k$. Functoriality of the chosen base factorization supplies $Z_k\to Z'_k$. Its commutation with $P_k\to Z_k$ and $Z_k\to Y_k$ proves compatibility with $i,p$; its commutation with the $L_kZ$ coprojection proves compatibility with every incoming arrow to $k$. For identity squares, the resulting comparison is the identity: this follows inductively from uniqueness on the latching colimit and pushout, and then from the identity law of the base factorization functor. For composable squares $(u,v):f\to f'$ and $(u',v'):f'\to f''$, write $q_k:P_k\to P'_k$ and $q'_k:P'_k\to P''_k$ for the induced pushout maps, and $z_k:Z_k\to Z'_k$, $z'_k:Z'_k\to Z''_k$ for the comparisons. The induction hypothesis gives that the comparison on each lower-degree $Z_j$ for the composite square is $z'_jz_j$. On every latching coprojection its induced map is therefore the composite of the two latching maps, by colimit uniqueness. On the $X_k$ coprojection the composite pushout map restricts to $u'_ku_k$, and on the $L_kZ$ coprojection it restricts to that composite latching map. Pushout uniqueness identifies it with $q'_kq_k$. The map on the codomains is $v'_kv_k$, so the square factored at $k$ is the composite of the squares $(q_k,v_k)$ and $(q'_k,v'_k)$. The composition law of the given base factorization functor now makes the resulting comparison exactly $z'_kz_k$. Hence Step 2 defines a functorial factorization on the entire arrow category, rather than unrelated objectwise choices.

source.place: Proof of Theorem 5.1.3, printed p. 122; functoriality expanded using universal cocones.

proof.text: Prove $C_K\perp R_K$ directly. Consider a square $f:A\to B$, $p:U\to V$, $a:A\to U$, $b:B\to V$ with $pa=bf$, where $f\in C_K$, $p\in R_K$. Inductively assume a natural lift $h_j:B_j\to U_j$ for degrees less than $n$, with $h_jf_j=a_j$ and $p_jh_j=b_j$. For $k$ of degree $n$ these maps give $L_kB\to U_k$, with component on $B_j$ equal to $U(j\to k)h_j$. It agrees on $L_kA$ with $A_k\xrightarrow{a_k}U_k$, because $h_jf_j=a_j$ and $a$ is natural. Thus there is a map $A_k\coprod_{L_kA}L_kB\to U_k$. This map, $b_k$, $\lambda_k(f)$ and $p_k$ form a commuting square: check on $A_k$ by $pa=bf$ and on each $B_j$ by $p_jh_j=b_j$ and naturality of $p,b$. The base WFS gives a lift $h_k:B_k\to U_k$. Its equations give $h_kf_k=a_k$, $p_kh_k=b_k$, and, on each $B_j$, $h_kB(j\to k)=U(j\to k)h_j$. This last equation is the required new naturality. The empty initial stage and the finite degree bound complete the lift.

source.place: Proposition 5.1.4, printed p. 121, written with the single pair (L,R).

proof.text: Since $\mathcal L={}^{\square}\mathcal R$ and $\mathcal R=\mathcal L^{\square}$ by hypothesis, [lem-coef-lifting-class-closure] makes both classes closed under arrow retracts. Evaluation preserves a diagram retraction componentwise, hence $R_K$ is retract-closed. For $C_K$, a square $f\to g$ induces a square $\lambda_k(f)\to\lambda_k(g)$: take the colimit maps on $L_k$, then the induced map of their pushout domains, and the component at $k$ on the codomains. Identities and composites are respected, since equality of maps out of each colimit or pushout is tested on its coprojections [def-weil-pbc-category-colimit]. Therefore an arrow retraction of $f$ from $g$ induces an arrow retraction of $\lambda_k(f)$ from $\lambda_k(g)$. Retract closure of $\mathcal L$ now proves retract closure of $C_K$. In particular these classes can be transported across arrow isomorphisms, which are arrow retractions with inverse.

source.place: Proof of Theorem 5.1.3, printed p. 122, retract check expanded; LiftingProperty.lean:51,56.

proof.text: The reverse lifting-class containments follow with explicit retractions. If $f:A\to B$ has the left lifting property against $R_K$, factor $f=pi$ as in Step 2. The square with top $i$, bottom $1_B$, left $f$ and right $p$ has a lift $s:B\to Z$ with $sf=i$, $ps=1_B$. The arrow maps $(1_A,s):f\to i$ and $(1_A,p):i\to f$ exhibit $f$ as a retract of $i$, so Step 5 gives $f\in C_K$. If instead $f$ has the right lifting property against $C_K$, the square with top $1_A$, bottom $p$, left $i$ and right $f$ has a lift $r:Z\to A$ with $ri=1_A$, $fr=p$. The arrow maps $(i,1_B):f\to p$ and $(r,1_B):p\to f$ exhibit $f$ as a retract of $p$, so $f\in R_K$. Together with Step 4 this identifies exactly both lifting classes. Steps 2-3 then give the claimed WFS with its functorial factorization. The retract closure used here is that supplied in Step 5 from [lem-coef-lifting-class-closure].

source.place: Hovey Lemma 1.1.9, printed p. 5, and end of proof of Theorem 5.1.3, printed p. 123; both retracts written explicitly.

proof.text: For $f:X\to Y$ in $C_K$, fix any $r:E\to F$ in $\mathcal R$ and a square from $\operatorname{colim}_Kf$ to $r$. Precomposing its horizontal maps with the colimit coprojections gives natural transformations $X\to\operatorname{const}E$ and $Y\to\operatorname{const}F$ forming a square with $f$ and the objectwise-$\mathcal R$ map $\operatorname{const}r$. Step 4 supplies a natural lift $Y\to\operatorname{const}E$. Its compatible components induce $d:\operatorname{colim}Y\to E$ by [def-weil-pbc-category-colimit]. The equations $d\operatorname{colim}f$ equal to the given top map and $rd$ equal to the given bottom map hold on every coprojection, hence hold by the uniqueness in that same universal property. This proves the left lifting property against every $r\in\mathcal R$, so $\operatorname{colim}f\in\mathcal L$. No adjoint-existence theorem or model-category theorem is being invoked: the cocone correspondence and both equations have just been constructed.

source.place: Corollary 5.1.5, printed pp. 121-122; Stacks 002F, categories-definition-colimit, for the explicit cocone argument.

proof.text: Fix $k$ and restrict $f$ along the domain projection $d:D_k\to K$. This is a finite direct indexing category with degree $\deg(j,a)=\deg j$. For its object $(j,a:j\to k)$, an object of the nonidentity slice into $(j,a)$ is a nonidentity $h:i\to j$ together with the necessarily determined $b=ah:i\to k$; $b$ is nonidentity since $\deg i<\deg j<\deg k$. Its morphisms are exactly commuting triangles between these $h$. Thus forgetting $b$ identifies this latching index category with $D_j$, including its domain functor to $K$; the inverse sends $h$ to the arrow $(i,ah)\to(j,a)$. Their compositions are identities. Consequently the relative latching map at $(j,a)$ for $f\circ d$ identifies, via the unique colimit and pushout isomorphisms of [def-weil-pbc-category-colimit], with $\lambda_j(f)$, and belongs to $\mathcal L$ by the arrow-isomorphism consequence of [lem-coef-lifting-class-closure]. Apply Step 7, which has already been proved for every finite direct category, to $D_k$ and $f\circ d$. This gives $L_kX\to L_kY$ in $\mathcal L$. Its pushout $X_k\to X_k\coprod_{L_kX}L_kY$ belongs to $\mathcal L$ by the pushout clause of that same closure node. Composing with $\lambda_k(f)\in\mathcal L$ gives $f_k\in\mathcal L$ by its composition clause. This proves the objectwise assertion without assuming it in the previous steps.

source.place: Remark 5.1.7, printed p. 123, with the slice/latching comparison expanded; Mathlib LiftingProperty.lean:61,72.

proof.text: If $K$ is empty, its diagram category has one object and one map. Both asserted classes contain that map, the factorization and lifts are the empty data, and its colimit map is the identity of the chosen initial object. This belongs to $\mathcal L={}^{\square}\mathcal R$ by the identity clause of [lem-coef-lifting-class-closure]. At an object with no incoming nonidentity arrow, the latching category is empty and its latching object initial, so the factorization in Step 2 and the lifting problem in Step 4 reduce to the base ones. Every argument used only finite size and increasing degree, so the identical constructions apply to any finite direct category, in particular to the possibly empty $D_k$ in Step 8.

source.place: Section 5.1, finite-degree and empty-category cases; Stacks 002F for the initial object as empty colimit.
